correspondence.component_scope: Western headward opening and south-turning feeder
correspondence.finding: The selected opening lies in a narrow mountain-floor drainage bordered by bare slopes and grassy valley margins. The visible stream corridor continues south-southeast and bends into the eastward passage. Small nearby upland ponds are outside this selected feeder. The imagery establishes the chosen opening and connection without supplying a separate headwater hydronym.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward mountain passage and joining northward valley
correspondence.finding: A continuous narrow stream valley runs east around the southern end of the intervening ridge, passes through the mountain notch and joins the broader drainage extending north-northeast. The selected successive bends and intermediate joins are visible. Scattered snow on adjacent ridges and tributary gullies does not constitute a selected glacier passage. No lake, reservoir or artificial transfer is needed to connect this section.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper northward course and bend into the middle valley
correspondence.finding: The selected course follows the continuous river floor north between mountain flanks, with side gullies and tributaries entering the same collector. Its short westward bend and renewed northeast turn correspond to the visible valley and channel belt. No separate through-link is inferred merely from watershed membership.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle northeast corridor and foothill joins
correspondence.finding: The middle view continuously depicts the northeast-trending river, broadening gravel bars, bends and western and eastern side-stream joins. The river leaves the confined upland valley for the lower rolling plain. Nearby ponds remain lateral to the selected corridor. Individual side tributaries are not assigned names from imagery.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower river and approach to the coastal delta
correspondence.finding: The selected northeast course stays within the continuous gravel-and-channel belt across the low plain. Side-stream confluences, abandoned meanders and adjacent ponds are visible before the river enters the low coastal distributary area. The regional named-delta identification is independently supplied by ARC403 rather than inferred from satellite appearance alone.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern delta distributary and actual marine ending
correspondence.finding: The lower view shows the river dividing across a pond- and wetland-rich delta. The selected eastward branch continues through the delta to an opening on its eastern coastal margin, followed by the rendered extension into adjoining marine water. This is the Blow delta setting: ARC403 places Trent Bay between Running River and Blow River, and Shoalwater Bay between the Blow delta and Tent Island. The extension beyond the coastal opening is a receiving-sea display segment, not a separately named river channel across the sea.

correspondence.component_scope: Whole-selection passage inventory
correspondence.finding: All selected parts and their joins are covered. The route contains a mountain feeder, narrow valley passage, broader river and coastal wetland/distributary passage. No selected large lake, reservoir, dam, canal, managed diversion or glacier crossing is visible in the materials read. Delta ponds and abandoned channels are not promoted to separately traversed named lakes. Source correspondence is geographic; present discharge, navigability and exact bank positions are not asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen northern opening and Wall Canyon Creek
correspondence.finding: The opening lies on the mapped southward intermittent drainage west of Badger Mountain. Repeated Wall Canyon Creek labels follow its same valley through the refuge boundary and the broad southward bend toward the Yellow Hills. The selected opening is on this labeled creek, rather than on nearby Cottonwood Creek or a spring point.
correspondence.name_scope: Wall Canyon Creek is the supported bounded upper hydronym.

correspondence.component_scope: Cottonwood junction and Pole Canyon passage into High Rock Creek
correspondence.finding: The originals show Cottonwood Creek joining the chosen Wall Canyon corridor from the east. The selection continues through the single deeply incised canyon south of that junction to the meeting with the separately mapped High Rock Creek trunk. The upper portion has less continuous blue linework than the canyon relief, but the enclosed canyon passage and its receiving junction are directly shown without an intervening basin crossing. The mapped Pole Canyon label applies to the canyon; it is not silently converted into a new river name.
correspondence.name_scope: Cottonwood Creek is adjoining tributary context; the selected canyon reach remains separately scoped. High Rock Creek is the receiving trunk.

correspondence.component_scope: High Rock Creek canyon and entry into the High Rock Lake receiving margin
correspondence.finding: The selected southward and southeastward bends follow the labeled High Rock Creek corridor, including the Mahogany Creek junction, the canyon mouth and the wet northern/western margin of High Rock Lake. Little High Rock Creek joins the same lake setting from the southwest and is not substituted for the selected northern entry.
correspondence.name_scope: High Rock Creek is the bounded river name; High Rock Lake is a separate waterbody.

correspondence.component_scope: High Rock Lake margin and northeast Fly Creek spillway
correspondence.finding: The detailed original draws an intermittent Fly Creek connection from the lake’s northeast margin through the adjacent col into the incised northeastern spillway. The generalized selected turn across the northern lake-margin setting corresponds to this same mapped lake-to-spillway geography. Sinclair’s own drainage account identifies the landslide-impounded lake, former pluvial overflow into Fly Creek and ordinary lake levels below the col. This supports the geographic passage while qualifying natural-system naming; present overflow is neither required nor asserted.
correspondence.name_scope: High Rock Lake and Fly Creek retain separate identities. Historical spillway geography is not treated as proof that the whole selection is one naturally named river.

correspondence.component_scope: Fly Creek canyon, lower marsh and Mud Meadow Reservoir entry
correspondence.finding: From the northeast lake margin the selection follows the mapped Fly Creek canyon to its flatter eastern fan and marsh, then enters Mud Meadow Reservoir where the northern Mud Meadow Creek collector also arrives. The originals depict the canyon bends, marsh approach and receiving waterbody together. No unseen canal transfer is used.
correspondence.name_scope: Fly Creek is the bounded intervening reach. Mud Meadow Reservoir is a distinct named receiving waterbody; the northern Mud Meadow Creek headwaters are not selected.

correspondence.component_scope: Mud Meadow Reservoir passage and southward outlet corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected southward passage crosses the narrow reservoir setting and follows the adjoining low outlet corridor below its southern end, along the western foot of Black Mountain and Big Mountain. Both the middle and lower originals show the same reservoir-to-valley continuation; no claim about dam operations or present water levels is made.
correspondence.name_scope: Mud Meadow Creek is directly labeled in the reservoir and receiving collector setting.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower collector, alluvial approach and upper western Black Rock Desert floor
correspondence.finding: The selected lower route occupies the continuously mapped axial receiving lowland south of the reservoir, with scattered wet patches, tributary fan entries and the Chipper Creek surroundings. The northwestern receiving corridor opens into the western Black Rock Desert floor between the Calico Mountains and the western flank of the Black Rock Range. The broad floor is continuous at ordinary scale; a separately drawn river thread across every fan or shallow pan is not required. Sinclair’s regional account independently places Mud Meadow Creek entering Black Rock Desert from the northwest.
correspondence.name_scope: Mud Meadow Creek remains the bounded lower-collector identity. Chipper Creek is an adjoining mapped drainage and is not assigned as the name of the selected whole.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual terminal in the western Black Rock Desert playa
correspondence.finding: The final selected southward continuation enters and remains within the mapped western Black Rock Desert playa and ends in its interior beside the elongated shallow-water patch. The endpoint and its preceding receiving floor are both covered. No extra ridge, separate lake-to-lake transfer or river line across the playa is inferred.
correspondence.name_scope: Black Rock Desert identifies the receiving geographic setting. No new lake name or river-name extension is assigned to the terminal floor.

correspondence.component_scope: selected opening
correspondence.finding: The selected southern opening occupies a low foothill drainage depression south of Malpaisillo. The original upper image shows its vegetated drainage corridor continuing north through the cultivated plain, then turning northwest/west into the upper river valley. The smallest opening has no independently established hydronym. Farmland, roads and drainage modification are acknowledged without inventing operation or perennial-flow facts.

correspondence.component_scope: olomega side upper valley
correspondence.finding: The selected route continues northwest through the southern valley below the Mina Santa Pancha setting. The Pacific-basin atlas distinguishes Olomega on this southern approach and Tecomapa on the adjacent northern/eastern drainage. Overlapping original imagery shows the continuous vegetated river valley and the joining-drainage zone. These reach names coexist within the representative Estero Real system; no exact name-change vertex is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: middle plain wetland passage
correspondence.finding: The corridor passes west/northwest across the low agricultural plain and road crossing into a sinuous floodplain and wetland-channel setting. The reserve base map carries the Estero Real corridor continuously across the lower part of this passage, while the overlapping upper/middle images expose the approach and the broadened wetland. Nearby meanders and side channels remain part of the receiving setting, rather than independently assigned river-name aliases.

correspondence.component_scope: lower estuary and managed margins
correspondence.finding: The reserve map labels Estero Real repeatedly through the large bends at and below Puerto Morazán. The original images show the same continuous widening estuarine channel, mangrove/wetland margins and extensive rectangular pond complexes. The plan independently maps shrimp-farming concessions along this estuary. The selected principal channel is retained through this managed landscape; no route through individual ponds or present sluice operation is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: terminal fragment and actual endpoint
correspondence.finding: The final fragment continues west along the broad Estero Real tidal arm. Its actual terminal lies within that broad lower-estuary receiving water, which the reserve map connects onward toward the Golfo de Fonseca. Both the supplied source and rendered endpoint settings are within this same marine-estuarine corridor at the research scale. The selected line is not extended to an invented outer-gulf mouth.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern highland opening and westward receiving join
correspondence.finding: The detailed original imagery shows the chosen opening in a highland swale southeast of the lake cluster. Its northwestward approach meets the westward drainage below that cluster, which turns southwest around the rocky spur into the same descending valley. The selected opening is not reassigned to a neighboring lake outlet merely because that outlet is more conspicuous. This establishes ordinary feeder-to-valley correspondence; no hydronym for the precise opening is inferred from imagery.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Unnamed selected headward feeder of the representative system

correspondence.component_scope: Upper descent through the Vichaycocha receiving valley
correspondence.finding: The upper image follows the same southwest-descending valley, its southward turn and intervening tributary mouths into the settled upper corridor. The study’s own map and modeled network distinguish Vichaycocha from the eastern Chicrín tributary and place their receiving junction on this upper river route. The selected course is the receiving valley, rather than a passage through the large eastern lake bodies.

correspondence.component_scope: Baños-side junction and turn into the westward main valley
correspondence.finding: The original imagery and study maps show the selected southward reach meeting the eastern Baños-side valley and turning west-southwest. The Baños and Quiles drainage network is separately depicted in the model; these are tributary inputs rather than alternative names imposed on the selected upper branch. The route remains continuously in the open river valley through this junction setting.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Transition to the representative Río Chancay-Huaral receiving corridor

correspondence.component_scope: Westward middle valley and Acos–Carac-side joins
correspondence.finding: The valley continues west through successive side-valley mouths toward the Acos and Carac junction setting. The independent model and Figure1 map provide the geographic continuation where small cloud patches affect the imagery. The selected westward and southwestward parts and their joins all occupy this same receiving corridor; the northern Carac approach remains a separately named tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwest middle corridor and Añasmayo–Huataya receiving sequence
correspondence.finding: The continuous mapped river follows the southwest-trending valley and local bend through the successive southern and northern tributary mouths. The study identifies Añasmayo on the left and Huataya on the right, and its own map/model network distinguish them from the selected trunk. The imagery confirms the intervening incised valley and broad local bend at ordinary corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Santo Domingo and lower valley opening
correspondence.finding: The selected corridor passes the study’s Santo Domingo control-station setting and continues southwest from the narrow mountain valley into the progressively wider cultivated valley. Both the source map and original lower image show continuous river-valley correspondence across all these parts. Irrigation branches and field subdivision are adjacent to the receiving river, not evidence of an unestablished inter-basin transfer.

correspondence.component_scope: Irrigated lower plain and southward river passage
correspondence.finding: The lower image shows the broad alluvial river bed continuing through the cultivated plain between Huaral-side and Aucallama-side lands, then turning south along the foothill margin. The study’s own network continues the river past the lower irrigation-demand nodes. The selected path remains in the same river corridor despite local braided bars, diversions and neighboring cultivated channels; no present allocation or flow rate is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Final southwest approach and actual Pacific mouth
correspondence.finding: The final selected part follows the same lower river corridor southwest through the coastal plain to the beach and Pacific receiving water south of the Chancay settlement setting. The completed original imagery shows the river-mouth approach and coastal receiving setting, corroborating the terminal depicted in the study map. This establishes the actual selected terminal without claiming an exact modern shoreline or a continuously open wetted mouth.
